title: How The Rosenhan Experiment Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck examine David Rosenhan's 1973 "On Being Sane in Insane Places" study, in which eight pseudo-patients, claiming to hear voices, were admitted to twelve US psychiatric hospitals and diagnosed with schizophrenia, then discharged with it "in remission." The episode covers the anti-psychiatry backlash, Rosenhan's own prior experience, the study design and staff/patient reactions, the follow-up challenge where a research hospital tried to spot pseudo-patients, the wider exposés of asylums, deinstitutionalization and the Community Mental Health Act, criticism of the study's methodology, and Susannah Cahalan's book The Great Pretender. Listener mail about mariachi music and five-part choral harmony closes the episode.
topics: On Being Sane in Insane Places
One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
Nellie Bly Ten Days in a Madhouse

segments.title: Psychiatry's crisis of confidence and the anti-psychiatry movement
segments.summary: Hosts set up mid-twentieth-century doubts about psychiatry, the anti-psychiatry movement, R. D. Laing's lecture, and Rosenhan's motivation to test whether psychiatrists could tell sane from insane.

segments.title: Study design: pseudo-patients
segments.summary: Rosenhan's earlier eight-day self-admission and the design of the study: pseudo-patients who falsely reported hearing voices, gave false names and occupations, then behaved normally, took notes openly, and carried writs of habeas corpus. One participant's data was dropped.
topics: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest

segments.title: Admissions and publication in Science
segments.summary: Details of the eight pseudo-patients admitted to twelve hospitals in five states, diagnosed mostly with schizophrenia, and the 1973 publication of the article in Science.

segments.title: Hospital life, staff and patient reactions
segments.summary: Staff failed to question the pseudo-patients, other patients saw through them, note-taking and cooperative behavior were pathologized, and staff rarely engaged with patients. Average stay was nineteen days, and most were discharged as schizophrenia in remission.

segments.title: The follow-up challenge hospital experiment
segments.summary: After Rosenhan was challenged, a research hospital was told pseudo-patients would arrive over three months. Staff flagged many admissions as suspected fakes, yet Rosenhan sent none, showing false positives.
topics: type I and type II errors

segments.title: Asylum exposés and deinstitutionalization policy
segments.summary: Earlier exposés of asylums by Nellie Bly, Titicut Follies, Willowbrook and Life magazine helped shift opinion. Kennedy's Community Mental Health Act was underfunded, and later Reagan-era cuts led to state hospital closures, homelessness, and prison populations for the mentally ill. The Penrose hypothesis is discussed.

segments.title: Criticism of the study and Cahalan's The Great Pretender
segments.summary: The study is viewed as non-rigorous by many, though it is valued for raising powerlessness and depersonalization. Susannah Cahalan's book The Great Pretender questioned Rosenhan's data and the existence of some pseudo-patients. Thomas Insel's comments on DSM diagnosis are noted.

segments.title: Listener mail: mariachi and five-part harmony
segments.summary: Listener mail about the band Mariachi El Bronx and a voice teacher's note that five-part and larger choral harmony is common, citing Spem in alium.
